newsitem.title: CHINA: China keeps nationalism leashed in islands dispute.
newsitem.headline: China keeps nationalism leashed in islands dispute.

text.p: Love of country and the defence of sovereignty may have become watchwords of China's communist leadership but when it comes to an island dispute with Japan, Beijing keeps its nationalism on a short leash.

While recent landings by Japanese politicians on disputed islands in the East China Sea have provoked popular outrage in Hong Kong and Taiwan, China has been careful to keep its own protests at the diplomatic level, analysts said on Sunday.

Beijing authorities, keen to promote patriotism while keeping public order, have shown no signs of easing curbs on public demonstrations over the contested islands, known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and the Senkakus in Japanese, they said.

"The danger of course is that if they were to allow anti-Japanese protest to form, there is a risk that the protests might eventually turn against something else," said one Western diplomat in Beijing.

Public expressions of anger against Tokyo could turn into criticism of the government's Sino-Japanese policies, and perhaps even become a focus for more general expresssions of dissatisfaction, the diplomat said.

The long-simmering Diaoyu dispute flared anew last week when Japanese opposition legislator Shingo Nishimura landed on the uninhabited islands, which Beijing and its island rival Taipei say have been Chinese territory for centuries.
A Japanese right-wing group last year already ignited fierce Chinese nationalist passions when it built a lighthouse on one of the Japanese-administered islands.
A Hong Kong activist on a flotilla to the islands drowned after he leapt into stormy seas to press China's claim.
Beijing expressed sympathy for the ideals of Hong Kong and Taiwan activists involved in such protests, but made sure their actions were not repeated by mainland counterparts.

China saw patriotism as a way to fill the vacuum left by the abandonment of much of its communist ideology during nearly two decades of economic reform, but the passions aroused by the islands dispute made Beijing nervous, analysts said.

Beijing's desire for smooth relations with Japan also dictated a measured response, even on an issue that touched a deep nerve among Chinese, who suffered hugely under Japanese occupation during World War Two.
"The government wants to set the agenda on Japan, which is a very important economic and political relationship," the Beijing-based diplomat said.

Prominent anti-Japanese activist Tong Zeng, who last year was pressured by officials into abandoning plans for public protests outside Tokyo's Beijing embassy, said he was still calling for diplomatic and military action over the Diaoyus.
Government officials had again made it clear that it wanted any action to be low-key, Tong said in a telephone interview.

"This time there hasn't been any direct (warning)... it's been indirect," he said. "The situation this year is a bit special... We will certainly put forward our view under the precondition of (keeping) stability."
Analysts said China welcomed the common ground that nationalism gave it with compatriots in rival Taiwan and in Hong Kong, which returns to Beijing rule on July 1.
But China's economic interest in preserving the delicate Sino-Japanese relationship was spelled out on Sunday by the official China Daily Business Weekly.
"The improvement of bilateral political ties will benefit the already booming economic ties between China and Japan," the newspaper said in a front page report.
A speech by President Jiang Zemin published in the People's Daily, mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party, was more likely to win praise from ardent nationalists.
"The Chinese people have never yielded to invaders," Jiang was quoted as saying in a months-old speech released on Sunday.
"Furious hatred of foreign invaders... (has) become our precious national character," he said.
